description: Parameterised final approaches for every element. An entry template is the fixed run-in an element requires: a length of specific edge, at a minimum speed, on a bounded curvature. The transition solver does NOT plan to an exact terminal pose - it plans to the START of the template, which turns a needle-thread into a fat target. See docs/composer-solver.md section 4.

notes.why_templates: Planning to an exact pose (position, heading, speed, foot, edge, all simultaneously) is a two-point boundary value problem and the reason naive approaches to this solver fail. Templates collapse it: the search only has to reach a dock region, and the template itself is a pre-solved, physically valid run-in that carries the skater the rest of the way.
notes.max_curvature: 1/metres. A lutz needs a LONG shallow back outside edge; too much curvature and the takeoff edge is unclear or the skater pre-rotates. This is why lutzes are entered down the long axis of the rink.
notes.speed_scaling: min_entry_speed_ms is quoted for a triple. Scale by rotations: singles x0.72, doubles x0.86, triples x1.0, quads x1.12.

long_axis.description: Approach along the 60 m dimension. Needed by templates over 10 m.

short_axis.description: Across the 30 m dimension. Only viable for short templates.

corner.description: The natural place to build speed with back crossovers.

templates.notes: Takes off from the landing edge of any jump, so as a second jump in a combination its template length collapses to zero - the previous jump's landing IS the entry.
Conventionally entered from a forward outside three turn onto the back inside edge. The solver is biased toward that primitive but not required to use it.

Edge-callable. The template holds a committed inside edge; drifting outside during it produces a lip. The solver flags a template it cannot hold within curvature bounds as a lip risk in the Composer UI.
The longest and most constrained template in the game, and the reason lutzes are entered down the long axis from a corner. A tight approach curve is exactly how a flutz happens.

The only FORWARD takeoff, so the template forces a direction change late in the transition. The solver almost always docks via a mohawk or three turn out of back crossovers, which is what real skaters do.
Note min_curvature: a spin entry needs a TIGHT hook, not a shallow one, because the entry curve is where the angular momentum comes from. This is the only template with a lower curvature bound.
Deliberately loose. A step sequence can start almost anywhere in almost any state - but it should start at a rink extremity, because the element itself must cover the full sheet.

exit_templates.note: The mirror image: every element ends in a known state, which is the transition's START. Jumps all exit right back outside, which is why the solver's start state is so often identical.
